P1.evidence: The application was acknowledged — 'I took a look at your application. I've got a bit of information about you' — though nothing specific was read back. The frame ran three of four parts: 'Really just want to understand more about you, where you're at with your fitness right now, what you're looking to accomplish, and then from there, if we can help, we can dive into all of the details about what we do.' Missing what is in the way and what he needs. Agreement was sought and given: 'That sounds good' → 'Yeah. No, sounds good.' The open question ran properly: 'in your opinion, what would you say is the biggest challenge that you're having with your fitness right now?' A clean, efficient opening — the best-formed P1 of the batch.

P2.evidence: Weight was obtained through the fat-loss question — 'how much weight would you say that you need to lose?' → 240 and could cut 20 — but age and height were never asked; the prospect said only 'I'm old'. Occupation was never asked at all, in eighteen minutes, so nothing is known about him professionally beyond that his workplace has a gym. Health conditions were never asked as a category. Injuries were volunteered in the prospect's very first sentence and the rep did follow up once on the knee — 'you said you tore your ACL. Is that still bothering you?' — accepted 'it's fine' and never probed the shoulder beyond the prospect's own mention of bench press, never asked what movements are restricted and never asked how long. Training week was covered well including days available. Diet was asked directly: 'do you have like a plan that you're following?' → 'No, nothing.' Sleep and energy never came up.

P3.evidence: The physical target was reached — jiu-jitsu, and specifically competing again — via 'what's got you back into it now after two years?' and 'Like competitive jujitsu? Did you do that before?' Credit is due on the bridge, which the rep asked twice in different forms: 'anything else that's going on as far as like what's got you back into it now after two years?' → 'Nope. Just want to get back into it', and again five minutes later, 'is there anything that we haven't spoke about on your end as far as like the reason why you want to do this now?' → 'No, I just want to get back into competitive shape.' Two clean attempts and two flat answers. What did not happen is the third attempt from a different angle, and none of the outward moves ran — no what does that do for you, no who else does that impact, nothing about his wife, no legacy or identity. The prospect is married and returning to a combat sport at 240 lb after knee surgery, and none of that was opened. The summary at 00:08:41 restated the situation without reframing it.

P4.evidence: Prior help was asked directly and well — 'Have you ever worked with a coach and gotten a program?' — producing the two personal training sessions and the generic plan he believed everyone received. The outcome was probed: 'did you get any results from it or like, how'd that go?', which surfaced that the results came from doing 75 Hard alongside it rather than from the plan. That is a genuinely useful thread and it was dropped there. Nobody asked why it did not stick, nobody asked what is actually in the way, the gap was never named by the prospect, and the scripted 'why can't you stick to it on your own' never ran. Given the prospect had just described two years of complete inactivity, this phase had the most to work with and got the least out of it.

P5.evidence: Never ran — the sixth consecutive sales call in this batch with no Consequence Frame. The material was unusually available here: two years lost, 240 lb, a reconstructed knee, a shoulder that will not press, and a stated ambition to compete in jiu-jitsu again. 'If nothing changes in two years, are you competing or are you watching?' was the whole call. Instead the rep asked twice for a why, accepted 'just want to get back into it', and went to price with nothing behind it.

P6.evidence: No commitment check. The rep did something structurally unusual instead: he pre-qualified budget before presenting, asking 'is that something that if everything made sense that you could do or maybe, maybe not, maybe need more time?' immediately after naming $9,000 and $6,000. That is a sensible instinct for saving time, and it is not P6 — it tests wallet, not belief. No question about whether he believes he can get there, no question about whether anything would stop him going all in, and no clear yes of any kind before the number. The prospect had asked for the price at minute nine and the rep gave it at minute ten, with discovery half-finished.

P11.evidence: No close was attempted on the coaching offer — the prospect declined it and the rep did not ask for the sale. The transaction that did occur was a self-serve Primal University signup, for which the playbook's payment, Trevor onboarding, agreement and welcome sequence do not apply. The rep did text the signup link during the call and confirmed the prospect received it, which is the one commitment step he executed anywhere in this batch.

objection_plays.detail: 'So I think maybe the timing's not right then' is the OD trigger almost verbatim, and not one move of the play ran. No 'things never slow down', no 'when does it actually become the right time', no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets', no 'the only thing you can control is right now'. The rep's next sentence was 'Well, I mean, we do have like other options, I guess.' Elapsed time between the objection landing and the downsell beginning: under thirty seconds.

'That's too much right now. I'm trying to work down some debt as well' is a money objection with a disclosed debt position behind it, and none of the play ran. No isolation, no 'finances aside, is there anything else', no certainty check, no permission for a financial conversation, and none of the six financial-picture questions. The only budget question asked was framed as a joke — 'if you have like $5 to your name, I might suggest going and watching YouTube' — and was used to route him to the cheaper product rather than to build a plan.

'the 6K is just, my wife would kill me' arrived late, after the downsell had already been accepted, but it is a clean spouse trigger and it was answered with 'Yeah, well, we don't want that.' None of the play ran. It also went unexamined as evidence that the real objection on the $6,000 was never money alone — worth noting because the rep had already closed the topic by then.

Script gap with a safety dimension the playbook does not cover. The prospect disclosed a reconstructed ACL and a load-intolerant shoulder in his opening sentence, and the rep's answer to affordability was to move him from a coached programme, where form review is the stated safeguard, to a self-directed video library where nobody sees him train. There is no play and no policy for when the downsell removes the supervision that the prospect's disclosed history warrants. That is a script and product-routing issue, not a rep failure.

notes: The cleanest opening in the batch and the fastest collapse. Frame, agreement and open question all ran properly, and the rep deserves credit for asking the deeper why twice rather than once. But price arrived at minute ten with P4 half-run and P5 and P6 not run at all, and when three separate objection triggers landed in sequence he played none of the five plays and downsold inside thirty seconds. Two coaching points. First, when a prospect answers the why question flatly twice, that is the signal to change the angle — try consequence, try the sport, try the wife — not the signal to price him. Second, and more important than the sale: a prospect who opens with a reconstructed ACL and a shoulder that cannot press needs the injury questions completed before any recommendation, and needs them most when the recommendation is the unsupervised product.
